note:
ISO 2026-W35 runs from August 24 through August 30. To find Mercury, first identify Leo, trace the Sickle, and locate Regulus in that pattern. Mercury lies about 2.7° away in ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot; use the finder to transfer from Regulus to the planet. Uranus is about 4.2° in ecliptic longitude from Aldebaran in Taurus.

**Naked eye:** 🌕 Full Moon · Fruit Moon — 04:18:32 UTC. Bright moonlight favors prominent stars and planets while reducing contrast on faint deep-sky objects. Use Albireo as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -11.3; direct motion; 83.8% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Opposition in ecliptic longitude Aug 28 04:18 UTC. Conjunction with Neptune in ecliptic longitude Aug 30 09:19 UTC. Conjunction with Pluto in ecliptic longitude Aug 25 16:10 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude -1.8; direct motion; 98.8% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Solar conjunction in ecliptic longitude Aug 27 17:03 UTC. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -4.5; direct motion; 43.8% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 1.3; direct motion; 92.3% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Ceres: Telescope; magnitude 9.0; direct motion; 97.5% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Jupiter: In solar glare; magnitude -1.8; direct motion; 99.9% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.5; retrograde motion; 99.9% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Uranus: Binoculars; magnitude 5.7; direct motion; 99.9% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.7; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Aug 30 09:19 UTC. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.5; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Aug 25 16:10 UTC.

**Binoculars:** Trace the charted figure of CrA, then identify β CrA at its plotted position. Trace the charted figure of Sgr, then identify Arkab Prior at its plotted position. Trace the charted figure of Sgr, then identify Arkab Posterior at its plotted position. Trace the charted figure of Sgr, then identify Rukbat at its plotted position. Trace the charted figure of Vul, then identify Anser at its plotted position. Trace the charted figure of Cyg, then identify Albireo B at its plotted position.

**Small telescope:** NGC 6752: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M56: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; PN G041.8-02.9: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Collinder 400: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

**Substantial telescope:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified as requiring a substantial telescope this week.

descriptors.name: Full Moon
descriptors.summary: Astronomical lunar phase near opposition to the Sun.
descriptors.body: Full Moon is the lunar phase in which the Moon and Sun are approximately opposite in geocentric ecliptic longitude, so the lunar disk is fully illuminated as seen from Earth.

story_candidates.dek: β CrA is a star in CrA of catalogue visual magnitude 4.10; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
The stored catalogue gives a visual magnitude of 4.10. This is a catalogue value, not a prediction of its brightness this week. Lower magnitudes mean brighter objects; sky brightness and altitude affect whether you can see the star.

Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 19h 10m and declination -39.3°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star rises and sets, reaching approximately 6° altitude at upper culmination. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved CrA constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.
